29. As far as the argument that no public witness was joined in the proceedings, it is suffice to note that usually public is not forthcoming to join such proceedings and nobody wants to get embroiled in legal matters and proceedings whereby he would have to repeatedly appear before the court to give evidence.

30. The fact that the percentage of colour is not mentioned in PA's report is irrelevant, as there is total prohibition of use of colour Tartrazine in Dal and the percentage is relevant only to conclude whether the product was rendered injurious and not otherwise.
As far as Section 2 (1a) (j) of PFA is concerned, it need not be shown that the product was rendered injurious but it is sufficient to show that colour was used though not permitted in the product.
Therefore, this argument has also no force.

Although, of course, the court must consider the fact that the product was not injurious to health and the same must be taken as Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 15/20 a mitigating circumstance while considering the aspect of sentencing.

sentences.text: On the other hand, it is argued by Ld. SPP for the Department that the sentencing cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences are changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged.
Definition of major offences like "adulteration" and "misbranding" have been changed.
FSSA have definition "substandard food", "food containing extraneous matter", "unsafe food" and "misbranded food".
Due to this reason, the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.

34. As far as the objection of Ld. SPP for State is concerned, in the present case, the offence was that the article/food i.e. Dal Arhar was found as being coloured with synthetic colour "Tartrazine".
This was violation of Rule 29 of PFA Rules and thus termed as adulteration in view of Section 2(ia)(j) of PFA Act and thus consequently punishable under Section 16(1) of PFA Act.
The charge was framed with these facts.
There was no charge in which it is stated that the said colour was injurious to health.
Had it been the case, then charge should have been under Section 16(1-A) (ii) of PFA Act.

35. As far as the application of Nemi Chand judgment (supra) is concerned, the same is based on the old judgment i.e. Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 17/20 T. Barai (supra) of Hon.
Supreme Court.

The relevant portion of the T. Barai judgment is as follows:-
(Para 25) - It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment, or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication.

In Michell v. Brown [(1958) 120 ER 909, 912:
32 LTOS 146 : 7 WR 80] Lord Campbell put the matter thus:
"It is well settled rule of construction that, if a later statute again describes an offence created by a former statute and affixes a different punishment, varying the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by the later statute; see also Smith v. Benabo [(1937) 1 All ER 523: (1937) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194] .

36. In Regina v. Youle [(1861) 158 ER 311, 315-16: 4 LT 299: 9 WR 637], Martin, B. said in the oft-quoted passage:

sentences.text: "If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offences, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act."

37. The rule is however subject to the limitation contained in Article 20(1) against ex post facto law providing for a greater punishment and has also no application where the offence described in the later Act is not the same as in the earlier Act i.e. when the essential ingredients of the two offences are different.

Moreover this particular aspect is stated as a illustration Vishambar Dayal Vs.
Department of PFA & Anr 18/20 in the same judgment in para 23 which is as follows:-
To illustrate, if Parliament were to reenact Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and provide that the punishment for an offence of murder shall be sentence for imprisonment for life instead of the present sentence of death or imprisonment for life

Department of PFA & Anr

sentences.text: , then it cannot be that the courts would still award a sentence of death even in pending cases.

38. So, in these circumstances, it can be safely said that while considering on the point of sentence,
the quantum of sentence in new Act i.e. FSSA is to be considered.

39. Now according to my aforesaid reasoning the offence of adding colour in food articles i.e. Dal Arhar, earlier punishable under Section 16(1A) of PFA Act is to be considered as an offence under Section 59(i) of FSSA Act for the purposes of awarding punishment.

The maximum punishment under Section 59(i) FSSA Act is imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months and also with fine which may extend to Rs.1 lac.
40.
It is not in dispute that the appellant/accused is almost 74 years old.
It is also claimed that he is a diabetic and has also faced trial in the present case for almost 15 years, including the present appeal.

I have also been informed that the accused has already deposited the fine of Rs.30,000/-
and he has discontinued the profession/business of Kirana store.

41. Further, it is noteworthy that the colour Tartrazine is permitted in some other food article falling under Rule 29 and Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 19/20 there is no opinion that the presence of colour in the Dal was injurious to health.

as also, he is a diabetic and no previous conviction has been proved against him, his sentence is reduced to the fine already paid and imprisonment till the rising of court.

Reliance is also being placed on the decision of Hon'ble Gujarat High Court in the case of State of Gujarat Vs. Laghadhirbhai Vaghijibhai Prajapati 2009 (2) 134 CCC (Gujarat), wherein, the Hon'ble Gujarat High Court analyzed the provisions contained in Rule 14 of the PF Rules and the relevant portion is quoted hereunder for ease of reference:-
"7.
Now, considering the provisions contained Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 8/20 in Rule 14 and appreciating the evidence on record, in the present case, it becomes clear that neither the Food Inspector Mr. Trivedi nor the panch Sanjay and nor the Sanitary Superintendent Kantilal Hargovinddas in their depositions clarified as to when, how and who cleaned the bottles, wherein the sample of groundnut oil was alleged to have been collected.
Reliance was also placed upon the judgment delivered by this court in the case of State of Gujarat v Sohanlal Trikamchand Shah reported in 2002(2) FAC 156, wherein almost identical principle was laid down as laid down in the above referred case.
Under such circumstances, even mere statement.
of the Food Inspector that the sample was collected in clean and dry bottle, would not amount to sufficient compliance of Rule 14.
It should be proved by leading cogent and positive evidence.
There is no explanation by the accused nor any suggestion that the colour Tartrazine could have entered into the sample from an unclean apparatus and how the apparatus would have had the said colour Tartrazine.
In the absence of any such further suggestion the mere admission of the witness that the Jhaba was not made clean and dry at the spot because it was already clean and dry has to be considered in correct perspective.

As far as Section 2 (1a) (j) of PFA is concerned, it need not be shown that the product was rendered injurious but it is sufficient to show that colour was used though not permitted in the product.
Although, of course, the court must consider the fact that the product was not injurious to health and the same must be taken as Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 15/20 a mitigating circumstance while considering the aspect of sentencing.
So, the finding of the trial court with respect to the conviction of accused under Section 2 (j)
& (m) of PFA Act 1954 read with Sec.16(1A) of PFA Act, is upheld.
It is further stated that the court should have passed the order on sentence as per the quantum/punishment mentioned in Food and Safety Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter called FSSA).
Due to this reason, the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.
This was violation of Rule 29 of PFA Rules and thus termed as adulteration in view of Section 2(ia)(j) of PFA Act and thus consequently punishable under Section 16(1) of PFA Act.
41. Further, it is noteworthy that the colour Tartrazine is permitted in some other food article falling under Rule 29 and Vishambar Dayal Vs. Department of PFA & Anr 19/20 there is no opinion that the presence of colour in the Dal was injurious to health.
